delimiter.

We need to talk about the request response cycle. It's got a posh name,
but actually it's not really a complex thing to understand. The request
response cycle is basically this. We start off with the client making an
HTTP request to the server. The server does some processing and sends an
HTTP response back to the client. So taking the example of an API, let's
look at this process in a bit more detail. So it starts with the client
and the client makes a request over HTTP and that request is full of
really useful information. It's going to tell us what method the client
is using and in our case that will be a get request. It's a get request
that you use when you are asking an API to give you some data.

It's going to tell us the path or the URL the request is being made to.

It might be that they want the entire data set in which case that

An event is a signal that something has happened. So, for example, a

received, and of course, there are many, many more events that we could
list. In this scrim, we're actually going to focus in on the event

listener functions. So when that named event occurs, in this case the

I think the last important thing to touch on with this before we move on

as it needs to be. In other words, if this component down here on the
bottom were the only one that needed state, then that's a great place to
put state. If its sibling needs access to that state, then moving it up
just one level is the best way. It might be tempting to think, well, I'm
going to stop refactoring this. I'm just going to shove my state at the
top of my application and then pass it down as many levels as I need to.

have state that is truly global across your entire application, that's
usually the time to start looking at one of those alternative solutions
that I mentioned like context redux or zustand or something like that.

The first one that I want to talk about is the concept of pure
functions. A pure function is one that if it's given the same inputs, it
will always produce the same outputs and running that function will
never have any kind of change elsewhere in your system. This is where
the concept of UI as a function of state comes from. All it simply means
is that the whole job of your components that you're writing are to take
input, which in one example might be incoming props from some above
component. And given those props, its entire purpose is to return a user
interface, some kind of DOM elements that display on the screen. And if
it's written correctly, no matter how many times your app component is
rendered, if the props are the same, then the UI that's produced will
always be the same.

Now, if the props that are coming in exist in a parent component and
that component changes those props somehow, maybe those props are
actually part of state in that parent component, then the change in
props will cause our app component to rerender and potentially produce
different results in the user interface. And this exact same principle
applies if what changes is an internal state change to our component.
Changing that state will then produce a new user interface. And as long
as that state changes the same, it doesn't matter how many times your
app component rerenders, it will always produce the same user interface.
And we talked early on about how React is in charge of doing all of the
nitty-gritty behind the scenes.

And we as developers just get to worry about making sure that our state
or our incoming props are being represented correctly so that what React
produces in the user interface is well represented correctly on the
page. As such, it's really important that the code inside of our
components is pure. In other words, it doesn't change anything outside
of its own system. And this leads us to the next main principle, which
is immutability. And we've talked about this. If we have a component

In Nex.js, there is a component that you can import called image and it
comes from next/image and it is an extension on top of the native img
element. So I can just drop in place the image component from Nex.js.
However, it does have some required properties that we have to make sure
we include. Of course, it needs to have a source just like any other
image. It also will send you a warning if you don't include any kind of
alt text. So we want to make sure we have that. But it's also required
for us to provide both a width property and a height property. However,
this is where the API for the image component differs from the native
img element. In the native HTML img element, when you provide width and
height, it actually sets the width and height to the sizes that you
provide.

The image component from Nex.js doesn't change the height or width of
the image. What they expect you to provide here is the native height and
width in pixels for the image that you're displaying. I believe the
original height and width is 742x 742 for this image. So, I would go
ahead and put those in here. Nex.js JS is not going to force the image
to be this exact size, but it does provide information for it so that it
knows how to resize it when it needs to and make sure the proportions
stay the same and a few other optimizations under the hood. Now, there
are other properties that you can use with the image component and you
can learn more about them from the documentation, but that's not really
what I want to get into at this point.

I do want to talk about some high-level optimizations that using the
image component provides. First of all, it will automatically resize the
image so that it will fit in its container correctly and make sure that
the proportions stay the same as well as converting the image file
itself to a more efficient format if the browser supports it. WEBP, for
example, is one of those more efficient formats that is that is designed
specifically for images on the web. The image component from Nex.js JS
will also automatically use lazy loading, which means the image will
only begin to load once that image is scrolled up into the viewport.
This way, if you have an imageheavy website where the images are further
down on the page, but it might happen often where the users don't scroll
down to see those images, but navigate somewhere else or use some other
feature.

Nex.js will avoid the network overhead by not downloading those images
until it's determined that they're actually needed in the view. Another
benefit of the image component from Nex.js JS is that it will help
prevent layout shift. This is when you load a new website, the images
have not yet loaded, but all of the text or other elements has loaded
and then only after the image begins to load does the text shift down
into a different place. X.js will reserve a space on your page for the
size of the image that is still incoming so that there isn't that jank
of things shifting around the page. So, the image component from Nex.js
is a really great component to use. However, I do have a little bit of
sad news.

Another neat thing that using the link component does is that Nex.js JS
will actually prefetch the upcoming route whenever that link is in view
on the web page. So if you can imagine having a long page that we need
to scroll down to, maybe way down here below there's a link, as soon as
that link becomes visible, Nex.js will prefetch that route in the
background so that by the time the user actually clicks that link, it
will already have been loaded in the background in the browser. That is
the default behavior for a link. Although, if there was maybe some
really expensive route that the users hardly ever click, you may decide
to improve the performance by manually turning the prefetch prop set to
false on the link element.

using the link component is that it will maintain React state between
the navigations. You can imagine if we have some kind of React state in
let's say the navbar of our project. Maybe it's maintaining a loggedin

example, to navigate from one route to the next, our navbar would have
to reestablish that state.

However, as the developer creating this, you need to work outside of the

called server components. A key aspect of server components is that the
code is run on the server. Now, I did put here that the code is only run
on the server. That's actually not strictly true, but it helps get the
point across.

Because the component is rendered on the server, it can perform any data
fetching before it does the rendering. Whereas in the client component,
it would mount and render the component first, then kick off the fetch
request. In server components, we can fetch the data and wait for it to
come back before we even begin the rendering process. This means we
don't have to use use effect or use state in order to deal with the
asynchronous nature of data fetching. We can simply await the data and
then use it in the markup. What we return from our React component will
include the data that we fetched. The code for doing this is
extraordinarily simple, at least compared to what you had to do in
clientside React using effect and use state.

comes back, I would set it into state. Changing state would rerender the
component now with the state holding the data from the API. And that's
when the user would finally see the data on the page. I'm just writing

Now I actually first heard about the client boundary from Josh Ko's

important to know that in Nex.js JS all components are by default server
components. In other words, anytime you import a component that you
created or are creating a page, if you don't include the use client
directive, then it will be considered a server component, which means
the code for that component will be run and rendered on the server and
then sent down as markup to the client or to the browser. Alternatively,
you can mark a component with the use client directive.

And that not only will mark that component, in this case, the layout
component as a client component, which means that the code for that
component won't be run on the server, but instead will be sent down to
the client or the browser for the browser to run that code. But a
crucial thing to understand is that when you include use client inside
of a component like this, it creates a boundary around itself and all of
its children that it imports and renders. In this sense, it creates a
boundary like you might see here where all of the code below use client
implicitly turns into client components and are no longer run on the
server, but instead are sent down to the browser for the browser to run
it.

Now, one thing I didn't mention is this form component uses something
called progressive enhancement, which means that if the user were ever
to find themselves without access to JavaScript, either the JavaScript
failed to load for whatever reason, maybe they have a really slow
internet connection and they are trying to interact with the page before
JavaScript has finished loading, or maybe even they have a browser
extension or browser setting that has turned off JavaScript altogether
for security or privacy concerns. This capital F form will automatically
downgrade itself to the native HTML form element and it will act exactly
the way that it was before we made this upgrade. It's called progressive
enhancement because we offer a path for the app to use an enhanced
version using capital F form with clientside navigation, but it also
provides a fallback which will make it so that your app doesn't
completely break if something were to go wrong when loading this
JavaScript.
